props.title: Titus

sections.content: Julie Taymor's Titus stands as one of cinema's most audacious Shakespeare adaptations, blending ancient Rome with 20th-century fascist aesthetics and surreal modern elements. Like Peter Greenaway's The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover (1989), it uses theatrical artifice and striking visuals to amplify its themes of revenge and corruption. Anthony Hopkins delivers a towering performance as Titus Andronicus in this hyper-stylized vision that makes Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet (1996) look tame by comparison.

sections.content: The film's stunning production design creates a world where ancient Roman columns share space with 1930s motorcycles and fascist architecture. This anachronistic approach echoes Derek Jarman's Edward II (1991) and The Tempest (1979) in using deliberate historical displacement to make Shakespeare's themes feel urgently contemporary. Taymor, coming from stage direction, brings theatrical techniques like masks, ritualized movement, and stark symbolic imagery that recall Peter Brook's landmark King Lear (1971).

The violence in Titus is both stylized and confrontational, forcing viewers to grapple with the cycle of revenge at the heart of Shakespeare's bloodiest play. The film's approach to graphic content shares DNA with Akira Kurosawa's Ran (1985) and Roman Polanski's Macbeth (1971) - other adaptations that don't shy away from depicting the full horror of their source material while maintaining artistic sophistication. sections.content: Taymor's visual innovations set new standards for bringing Shakespeare to screen. Her use of surreal imagery and dream sequences builds on techniques pioneered in Orson Welles' Chimes at Midnight (1965) and Kenneth Branagh's Hamlet (1996). The film's striking color palette and composition draws from Italian horror masters like Mario Bava, while its mixing of historical periods recalls O (2001), which relocated Othello to a modern American high school.
